newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala 9-month banana exports up 5.7 percent.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala 9-month banana exports up 5.7 percent.

text.p: The volume of Guatemala's banana exports rose 5.7 percent to 10.34 million quintales, or 100-pound bundles, in the first nine months of 1996 comapred to the year before, the leader of Guatemala's Banana Producers Association said Friday.
The figure compares to 9.78 million quintales for the first three quarters of last year.

Meanwhile, the value of Guatemala's banana exports rose 14.8 percent to $117 million in the first nine months of 1996 compared to the same period a year ago, when it was $103 million, the association said.
Nonetheless, it has been a bad year for Guatamalan banana producers, the group said.

"The year has been pretty bad in relation to floods, a lot of labor problems and as far as diseases ... sigatoka has hurt productivity a lot," Javier Flores, director of the Banana Producers Association, told Reuters in an interview.
According to Flores the increase in exports and production is due to new plantations built by Standard Fruit de Guatemala and other growers on Guatemala's southern coast.
Flores said Guatemala will export a total of 30 million boxes of bananas in 1996 and predicts 30 million to 33 million boxes exported in 1997.

Flores did not know what percentage of the 1996 crop was affected by flooding in August and September or by sigatoka, a fungus. But he said exports would have been higher if those factors had not affected production.

Flores said production had slowed for his employer, the Compania Bananera Guatemalteca Independiente (Cobigua), Guatemala's second-largest producer, because labor unions are negotiating pay raises and producers want to implement production-based pay scales.
Major banana producers here are Bandegua, which sells to Del Monte, Cobigua which sells to Chiquita Brands International and Standard Fruit de Guatemala, which sells to Dole Food Co.
Flores said it was important for Guatemalan producers to improve quality to compete with other countries that sell to the United States, Guatemala's main market.

He said much would depend on the results of continuing negotiations before the World Trade Organization regarding the European Union's import rules, which impose high tariffs on bananas imported from Latin America over a yearly cuota.
Flores said banana production will not expand significantly in Guatemala next year. He said there were some new plantations on the southwestern coast in the department of San Marcos.

But most new areas of production were substituting areas going out of production in the traditional northern area of banana plantations, in the department of Izabal, due to flooding and other factors, he said.
